entities.summary:
Jean-François Marie de Surville was a merchant captain with the French East India Company. He commanded a voyage of exploration to the Pacific in 1769–70, becoming the first European to sight the coast of New Zealand. This expedition had a profound impact on the French presence in the Pacific and paved the way for further French exploration and colonization of the region. De Surville's voyage also marked a significant milestone in the history of European exploration, as it demonstrated the feasibility of navigating the Pacific and sparked a renewed interest in the region. The voyage's legacy can be seen in the establishment of the first French settlement in New Zealand, which was established in 1769, shortly after de Surville's voyage. 

Jean-François Marie de Surville was born on January 18, 1717, in Port-Louis, and died on April 7, 1770. He was a key figure in the French East India Company's efforts to expand its presence in the Pacific. De Surville's exploits have been immortalized in literature and popular culture, with his name becoming synonymous with French exploration of the Pacific.

De Surville's voyage of 1769–70 was a pivotal moment in the history of European exploration, as it demonstrated the feasibility of navigating the Pacific and sparked a renewed interest in the region. The voyage's legacy can be seen in the establishment of the first French settlement in New Zealand, which was established in 1769, shortly after de Surville's voyage.

De Surville's voyage also had significant consequences for the indigenous populations of New Zealand, who had not previously encountered Europeans. The French presence in the region had a profound impact on the native cultures and ways of life, leading to the displacement and marginalization of many indigenous peoples.
